Polynomials

A polynomial is a curve with a story. Where it crosses the x-axis tells you its zeroes; its coefficients tell you their sum and product. This chapter connects those two facts — the picture and the algebra.

0, 1 or 2 zeroessum = −b/aproduct = c/a12 NCERT questions
The curve shows you where the zeroes are. The coefficients tell you what they add up to.

2.1 · Getting the words right

02Degree decides the shape

The degree is the highest power of x in the polynomial. It is also the number of times the curve is allowed to bend — which is why it controls how many zeroes you can have.

Degree 1

Linear · ax + b

A straight line. It crosses the x-axis exactly once, so exactly one zero.

zero = −b/a

Degree 2

Quadratic · ax² + bx + c

A parabola — a U or an upside-down U. It can meet the axis twice, once, or not at all.

at most 2 zeroes

Degree 3

Cubic · ax³ + bx² + cx + d

An S-shaped curve. It can cross the axis up to three times.

at most 3 zeroes

A zero of p(x) is a number k with p(k) = 0. That is all. For p(x) = x² − 3x − 4, putting x = 4 gives 16 − 12 − 4 = 0, so 4 is a zero; putting x = 2 gives −6, so 2 is not.

The three possible pictures

cuts twice → 2 zeroes
touches once → 1 zero (twice)
never meets → no real zero

Why a quadratic stops at two Its degree is 2, and a polynomial of degree n can have at most n zeroes. A cubic can have three, and the S-shaped curve below shows how.
2.3 · Zeroes and coefficients

04The sum and the product

If α and β are the zeroes of ax² + bx + c, then the two coefficients b and c are secretly carrying their sum and their product.

α + β = −ba     αβ = ca
Interactive · Check the relationship

Sum of zeroes

If the discriminant is negative the zeroes are not real, and this lab will say so instead of inventing numbers.

Making a polynomial from its zeroes

Work backwards. If the sum is S and the product is P, then a quadratic with those zeroes is

k(x² − Sx + P)

Any non-zero k works; k = 1 gives the simplest one. This is exactly Example 4 in the book.

And for a cubic

With zeroes α, β, γ of ax³ + bx² + cx + d:

α+β+γ = −b/a
αβ+βγ+γα = c/a
αβγ = −d/a

The signs alternate: minus, plus, minus.

Worked examples

05Two examples, step by step

Example · Zeroes of 2x² − 8x + 6

Step-through · splitting the middle term
The method you will use most often.
Multiply a and c. 2 × 6 = 12. We need two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to −8.
They are −6 and −2. Split the middle term: 2x² − 6x − 2x + 6.
Group. 2x(x − 3) − 2(x − 3) = (2x − 2)(x − 3) = 2(x − 1)(x − 3).
Zeroes are 1 and 3. Check: sum = 4 = −(−8)/2 ✓, product = 3 = 6/2 ✓.

Example · A quadratic with sum 3 and product 2

Step-through · working backwards
From the numbers you want to the polynomial you need.
Use the pattern. p(x) = x² − (sum)x + (product).
Substitute. x² − 3x + 2.
Check by factorising. x² − 3x + 2 = (x − 1)(x − 2), so the zeroes are 1 and 2 — sum 3, product 2 ✓.

Before the exam

07Four traps

01

Zero is not “no solution”

A zero of p(x) is a value of x, not the value of the polynomial. p(2) = 0 means 2 is the zero.

02

Mind the signs

α + β = −b/a. Dropping the minus is the most common single mistake here.

03

Touching counts

If the curve only touches the axis, that point is still a zero — it is just counted twice.

04

k is allowed

Many quadratics share the same zeroes. When asked to “find a quadratic”, any non-zero multiple is correct.

Doubts, answered

10Frequently asked questions

For polynomials the two words mean the same thing: a value that makes the expression zero. “Root” is more often used when the expression is an equation.

Because its parabola may float entirely above or below the x-axis. In that case b² − 4ac is negative and the zeroes are not real numbers — but they still exist in a wider number system.

Yes, any real number. 2x + 3 has the zero −3/2, and 3x² + 5x − 2 has zeroes 1/3 and −2.

If a is positive the parabola opens upwards like a cup; if a is negative it opens downwards. If a is zero it is not a quadratic at all — it becomes a straight line.

Multiply a by c. Find two numbers that multiply to that product and add to b. Split b using them, then group in pairs. Practice makes the pair obvious within seconds.

A zero is exactly a point where y = 0, and y = 0 is the x-axis. So counting zeroes is the same as counting where the curve meets that axis.

11Important questions to master

3x − 7 = 0 → x = 7/3.

No real zeroes.

Sum = 5/3, product = 2/3.

Sum = 1, product = −12 → x² − x − 12.

4u(u + 2) = 0 → u = 0 or u = −2.

Sum = −2 = −8/4 ✓; product = 0 = 0/4 ✓.

Zeroes are 4 and −2, so α − β = 6. (In general (α − β)² = (α + β)² − 4αβ = 4 + 32 = 36.)

Let the zeroes be 2m and 3m. Product 6m² = 6 → m = 1.

Sum = 5m = 5 = k. So k = 5.

α + β = −7, αβ = 12.

New sum = (α + β)/αβ = −7/12; new product = 1/12.

Polynomial: x² + (7/12)x + 1/12, or 12x² + 7x + 1.

Chapter summary

13Five lines to revise

  • Degrees 1, 2, 3 are called linear, quadratic and cubic.
  • Zeroes are the x-coordinates where the graph meets the x-axis.
  • A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes.
  • Quadratic: α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a.
  • Cubic: sum = −b/a, pair-sum = c/a, product = −d/a.
